introLesson.title: Introduction to To Build a Fire

sections.authorBiography: Jack London was born in San Francisco on 12 January 1876 and grew up poor in Oakland, working in a cannery, as an oyster pirate and as a sailor, and riding the rails as a hobo. In 1897 he joined the Klondike Gold Rush in the Yukon; he found no gold but found his subject. The Call of the Wild (1903) made him one of the best-paid writers in the world. A socialist and adventurer, he wrote some 50 books before his death at his California ranch on 22 November 1916.
sections.historicalContext: The story is set on the Yukon Trail during the Klondike Gold Rush (1896–99), where temperatures can fall below −50°F. London went to the Klondike in 1897 and nearly died of scurvy.

publicationAndReception.publication: The best-known version was published in The Century Magazine in August 1908; an earlier, quite different version for boys appeared in The Youth's Companion in 1902, in which the man survives.
publicationAndReception.now: A classic of naturalism, studied for man-versus-nature conflict and its indifferent universe.

sections.overview: An unnamed newcomer sets out alone, with only a husky dog, to walk to a mining camp on a day of extreme cold, ignoring an old-timer's warning.
sections.whyItMatters: It is a model of naturalism and of suspense from a simple plot, and a reminder to respect nature.

spoilerOverview.text: He falls through ice, gets his feet wet, and fails to keep a fire going; he freezes to death, and the dog goes on to the camp.

segments.script: About the author. Jack London was born in San Francisco on 12 January 1876 and grew up poor in Oakland, working in a cannery, as an oyster pirate and as a sailor, and riding the rails as a hobo. In 1897 he joined the Klondike Gold Rush in the Yukon; he found no gold but found his subject. The Call of the Wild (1903) made him one of the best-paid writers in the world. A socialist and adventurer, he wrote some 50 books before his death at his California ranch on 22 November 1916. The world of the book. The story is set on the Yukon Trail during the Klondike Gold Rush (1896–99), where temperatures can fall below −50°F. London went to the Klondike in 1897 and nearly died of scurvy. Publication and reception. The best-known version was published in The Century Magazine in August 1908; an earlier, quite different version for boys appeared in The Youth's Companion in 1902, in which the man survives. Then: Widely read. Now: A classic of naturalism, studied for man-versus-nature conflict and its indifferent universe.

lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 8–11 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in To Build a Fire.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about To Build a Fire: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

items.prompt: What advice did the old-timer from Sulphur Creek give?
options: Never travel alone below fifty below

items.prompt: What puts out the man's first big fire?
options: Snow falling from the spruce tree above

items.prompt: What does the dog rely on?
What does the dog do at the end?
options: Heads toward the camp and other food-providers

items.prompt: In the line “It grew like an avalanche, and it descended without warning upon the man and the fire, and the fire was blotted out!”, what does “avalanche” most nearly mean?
options: partial or total lack of sensation in a part of the body; a symptom of nerve damage or dysfunction
a slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain

items.prompt: In the line “He did not expose his fingers more than a minute, and was astonished at the swift numbness that smote them.”, what does “numbness” most nearly mean?
options: a slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain
partial or total lack of sensation in a part of the body; a symptom of nerve damage or dysfunction

items.prompt: As used in the story (“It grew like an avalanche, and it descended without warning upon the man and the fire, and the fire was blotted out!”), what does “avalanche” mean?
options: a slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain
extend out or project in space
chew (food); to bite and grind with the teeth
partial or total lack of sensation in a part of the body; a symptom of nerve damage or dysfunction

items.prompt: As used in the story (“He did not expose his fingers more than a minute, and was astonished at the swift numbness that smote them.”), what does “numbness” mean?
options: partial or total lack of sensation in a part of the body; a symptom of nerve damage or dysfunction
get involved, so as to alter or hinder an action, or through force or threat of force

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Usually the snow above the hidden pools had a sunken, candied appearance that advertised the danger.”), what does “advertised” mean?
options: talk indistinctly; usually in a low voice
first one and then the other

items.prompt: As used in the story (“The man's red beard and mustache were likewise frosted, but more solidly, the deposit taking the form of ice and increasing with every warm,”), what does “exhaled” mean?
options: chew (food); to bite and grind with the teeth
a slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain
extend out or project in space

items.prompt: As used in the story (“As for lunch, he pressed his hand against the protruding bundle under his jacket.”), what does “protruding” mean?
options: extend out or project in space

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what To Build a Fire teaches about nature's indifference. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Jack London develops nature's indifference in To Build a Fire. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Jack London develops nature's indifference across To Build a Fire. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of To Build a Fire (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of nature's indifference. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of nature's indifference in To Build a Fire. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Jack London's choices in To Build a Fire (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of nature's indifference, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places To Build a Fire's treatment of nature's indifference in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on nature's indifference in To Build a Fire that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on nature's indifference in To Build a Fire. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about nature's indifference in To Build a Fire, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
